title: Chapter 17
paragraphs: Without meaning to, Alexey Alexandrovitch went back over the conversations during and after dinner as he returned to his solitary room. Darya Alexandrovna's words about forgiveness had only irritated him. Whether the Christian precept applied to his case was too difficult a question to be tossed around in passing, and besides, he had long ago settled it for himself in the negative. Of everything that had been said, what stuck in his memory was the line from that stupid, good-natured Turovtsin — "_Acted like a man, he did! Called him out and shot him!_" Everyone, apparently, had felt the same, even if politeness kept them from saying so.

"But the matter is settled, there's no point dwelling on it," Alexey Alexandrovitch told himself. Thinking only of the journey ahead and the revision work he had to do, he went into his room and asked the porter who had shown him up where his valet was. The porter answered that the man had only just stepped out. Alexey Alexandrovitch ordered tea brought to him, sat down at the table, took the guidebook, and began going over the route of his journey.
"Two telegrams," said his valet, coming into the room. "I beg your pardon, your excellency — I'd only just stepped out for a minute."

Alexey Alexandrovitch took the telegrams and opened them. The first announced Stremov's appointment to the very post that Karenin had wanted. He threw the telegram down and, flushing slightly, got up and began to pace the room. "_Quos vult perdere dementat_," he said, meaning by _quos_ those responsible for the appointment. It wasn't so much that he hadn't been given the post, or that he had been pointedly passed over; what astonished him was that they couldn't see how the wordy phrase-monger Stremov was the last man fit for it. How could they fail to notice that they were undermining themselves and damaging their own _prestige_ with this choice?

"More of the same," he muttered bitterly, opening the second telegram. The telegram was from his wife. Her name, written in blue pencil — "Anna" — was the first thing his eye caught. "I am dying; I beg, I implore you to come. I shall die easier with your forgiveness," he read. He smiled contemptuously and threw the telegram down. That this was a trick and a fraud, of that, he thought for the first moment, there could be no doubt.

"There's no deceit she wouldn't stoop to. She was near her confinement. Perhaps it is the confinement. But what would they be after? To legitimize the child, to compromise me, and block the divorce," he thought. "But there was something in it: I am dying...." He read the telegram again, and suddenly the plain meaning of the words struck him.

"And what if it's true?" he said to himself. "If it's true that at the moment of agony, of nearness to death, she really is repentant, and I treat it as a trick and refuse to go? That wouldn't only be cruel — and everyone would blame me — it would be foolish of me."
"Piotr, call a coach — I'm going to Petersburg," he said to his servant.

Alexey Alexandrovitch resolved that he would go to Petersburg and see his wife. If her illness turned out to be a trick, he would say nothing and leave again. If she really was in danger and wanted to see him before she died, he would forgive her if he found her alive and pay her the last respects if he was too late.
On the whole journey he gave no further thought to what he ought to do.

Weary and unclean from a night spent in the train, in the early morning fog of Petersburg, Alexey Alexandrovitch drove along the deserted Nevsky, staring straight ahead, not thinking about what awaited him. He could not bring himself to think about it, because every time he pictured what would happen, he couldn't push away the recognition that her death would at once remove every difficulty in his position. Bakers, shuttered shops, night cabbies, porters sweeping the pavements all flashed past, and he watched it all, trying to smother the thought of what was ahead and what he didn't dare hope for — and yet was hoping for. He drove up to the steps. A sledge and a carriage with a sleeping coachman stood at the entrance. As he stepped into the hall, Alexey Alexandrovitch fished out, as it were, from the farthest corner of his brain his resolve, and made himself fully master of it. Its substance ran: "If it's a trick, then calm contempt, and leave. If it's true, do what's proper."
The porter opened the door before Alexey Alexandrovitch could ring. The porter, Kapitonitch, looked odd in an old coat, without a tie, and in slippers.
"How is your mistress?"
"A successful confinement yesterday."
Alexey Alexandrovitch stopped short and went white. He felt, distinctly now, how intensely he had been hoping for her death.
"And how is she?"
Korney, in his morning apron, came hurrying down the stairs.
"Very ill," he answered. "There was a consultation yesterday, and the doctor is here now."
"Take my things," said Alexey Alexandrovitch, and, feeling a slight relief at the news that there was still some hope of her death, he stepped into the hall.
On the hat-stand was a military overcoat. Alexey Alexandrovitch noticed it and asked:
"Who is here?"
"The doctor, the midwife, and Count Vronsky."
Alexey Alexandrovitch walked through into the inner rooms.
There was no one in the drawing-room; at the sound of his footsteps, the midwife came out of Anna's boudoir, in a cap with lilac ribbons.
She went up to Alexey Alexandrovitch and, with the familiarity that the nearness of death allows, took him by the arm and drew him toward the bedroom.
"Thank God you've come! She talks of nothing but you," she said.
"Bring the ice — quickly!" came the doctor's curt voice from the bedroom.
Alexey Alexandrovitch went into her boudoir.

At the table, sitting sideways in a low chair, was Vronsky, his face buried in his hands, weeping. At the sound of the doctor's voice he jumped up, lowered his hands, and saw Alexey Alexandrovitch. At the sight of the husband, he was so stricken that he sat down again, pulling his head down between his shoulders as if he wanted to vanish; but he forced himself, stood up, and said:
"She is dying. The doctors say there is no hope. I am entirely in your power, only let me stay here.... I'm at your disposal. I...."

Alexey Alexandrovitch, seeing Vronsky's tears, felt that rush of nervous emotion that the suffering of others always stirred in him; turning his face away, he hurried toward the door without waiting to hear the rest. From the bedroom came the sound of Anna's voice saying something. Her voice was lively, eager, with strikingly clear intonations. Alexey Alexandrovitch entered the bedroom and went up to the bed. She was lying with her face turned toward him. Her cheeks were flushed crimson, her eyes glittered, her little white hands, thrust out from the sleeves of her dressing-gown, played with the quilt, twisting it in her fingers. She looked not only well and blooming but in the happiest frame of mind. She was talking quickly, musically, with unusually precise articulation and expressive intonation.

"For Alexey — I mean Alexey Alexandrovitch (what a strange and dreadful thing it is, that both of them are Alexey, isn't it?) — Alexey wouldn't refuse me. I should forget; he would forgive.... But why doesn't he come? He's so good he doesn't even know how good he is. Oh, my God, what agony! Quick — give me some water! Oh, that will be bad for her, my little girl! All right then, give her to a nurse. Yes, I agree, that really is better. He'll be coming; it will hurt him to see her. Give her to the nurse."
"Anna Arkadyevna, he has come. Here he is!" said the midwife, trying to draw her attention to Alexey Alexandrovitch.

"Oh, what nonsense!" Anna went on, not seeing her husband. "No, give her to me — give me my little one! He hasn't come yet. You say he won't forgive me, because you don't know him. Nobody knows him. Only I do, and even for me it was hard. His eyes — I should know them — Seryozha has just the same eyes — and I can't bear to look at them because of it. Has Seryozha had his dinner? I know everyone will forget about him. He would not forget. Seryozha must be moved into the corner room, and Mariette must be asked to sleep with him."
Suddenly she shrank back, fell silent; and in terror, as if expecting a blow, as if shielding herself, she raised her hands to her face. She had seen her husband.

"No, no!" she said. "I'm not afraid of him; I'm afraid of death. Alexey, come here. I'm in a hurry, because I have no time, I have not long to live; the fever will start any minute and I'll understand nothing more. Right now I understand, I understand everything, I see it all!"

Alexey Alexandrovitch's lined face wore an expression of agony; he took her by the hand and tried to say something, but couldn't get the words out; his lower lip trembled, but he kept on wrestling with his emotion and only glanced at her now and then. And each time he glanced at her, he saw her eyes resting on him with a passionate, triumphant tenderness he had never seen in them before.

"Wait a minute, you don't know.... Stay a little, stay!..." She paused, as if gathering her thoughts. "Yes," she began; "yes, yes, yes. This is what I wanted to say. Don't be surprised at me. I'm still the same.... But there is another woman in me, I'm afraid of her: she loved that man, and I tried to hate you, and couldn't forget about the woman I used to be. I'm not her. Now I'm my real self, all of me. I'm dying now — I know I'm going to die, ask him. Even now I can feel — see, the weights on my feet, on my hands, on my fingers. My fingers — see how huge they are! But this will all be over soon.... Only one thing I want: forgive me, forgive me completely. I'm terrible, but my old nurse used to tell me about that holy martyr — what was her name? She was worse. And I'll go to Rome; there's a wilderness there, and I'll be no trouble to anyone, only I'll take Seryozha and the little one.... No, you can't forgive me! I know — it can't be forgiven! No, no, go away, you're too good!" She held his hand in one burning hand, while she pushed him away with the other.

Alexey Alexandrovitch's nervous agitation kept rising, until he stopped struggling against it. He suddenly felt that what he had thought of as nervous agitation was on the contrary a blissful spiritual state that gave him, all at once, a new happiness he had never known. He didn't think that the Christian law he had been trying to live by all his life commanded him to forgive and love his enemies; but a glad feeling of love and forgiveness toward his enemies filled his heart. He knelt down and, laying his head in the bend of her arm, which burned him through the sleeve as though with fire, he sobbed like a small child. She put her arm around his head, drew him closer, and with defiant pride raised her eyes.
"There he is. I knew him! Now, forgive me, everyone, forgive me!... They've come again — why don't they leave?... Oh, take these cloaks off me!"
The doctor loosened her hands, settled her carefully on the pillow, and covered her up to the shoulders. She lay back submissively and looked ahead of her with shining eyes.

"Remember one thing — that all I needed was forgiveness, and I want nothing more.... Why doesn't _he_ come?" she said, turning toward the door where Vronsky stood. "Do come, do come! Give him your hand."
Vronsky came up to the side of the bed and, seeing Anna, hid his face in his hands again.
"Uncover your face — look at him! He's a saint," she said. "Oh — uncover your face, do!" she said angrily. "Alexey Alexandrovitch, do uncover his face! I want to see him."
Alexey Alexandrovitch took Vronsky's hands and drew them away from his face, which was dreadful with the expression of agony and shame on it.
"Give him your hand. Forgive him."
Alexey Alexandrovitch held out his hand, not trying to hold back the tears that streamed from his eyes.

"Thank God, thank God!" she said, "now everything is ready. Just to stretch my legs a little. There — that's lovely. How badly these flowers are done — they don't look like violets at all," she said, pointing to the hangings. "My God, my God! When will it end? Give me some morphine. Doctor, give me some morphine! Oh, my God, my God!"
And she tossed about on the bed.

The doctors said it was puerperal fever, and that there were ninety-nine chances out of a hundred that it would end in death. All day long there was fever, delirium, and loss of consciousness. By midnight the patient lay unconscious, and almost without pulse.
The end was expected at any moment.

Vronsky had gone home, but in the morning he came back to inquire, and Alexey Alexandrovitch, meeting him in the hall, said: "You'd better stay; she might ask for you," and led him himself to his wife's boudoir. Toward morning there was a return of the excitement, the rapid thought and talk, and again it ended in unconsciousness. On the third day it was the same, and the doctors said there was hope. That day Alexey Alexandrovitch went into the boudoir where Vronsky was sitting, shut the door, and sat down opposite him.

"Alexey Alexandrovitch," said Vronsky, sensing that some statement of the situation was coming, "I can't speak, I can't take it in. Spare me! However hard it is for you, believe me, it is more terrible for me."
He would have stood up, but Alexey Alexandrovitch took him by the hand and said:

"Please hear me out — it's necessary. I have to explain my feelings, the feelings that have guided me and will guide me, so that you won't be in any doubt about me. You know that I had resolved on a divorce and had even begun proceedings. I won't hide from you that when I started this, I was full of uncertainty, full of misery; I'll admit that I was pursued by a desire to take revenge on you and on her. When I got the telegram, I came here with the same feelings; I'll say more — I longed for her death. But...." He paused, weighing whether to reveal what he felt to him. "But I saw her and forgave her. And the happiness of forgiveness has revealed my duty to me. I forgive completely. I would offer the other cheek, I would give my cloak if my coat were taken. I only pray to God that he won't take from me the bliss of forgiveness!"
Tears stood in his eyes, and Vronsky was struck by the luminous, serene look in them.

"This is where I stand: you can trample me in the mud, make me the laughing-stock of the world, I will not abandon her, and I will never speak a word of reproach to you," Alexey Alexandrovitch went on. "My duty is clearly laid out for me; I ought to be with her, and I will be. If she wants to see you, I'll let you know, but for now I think it would be better for you to go away."

He stood up, and sobs cut off his words. Vronsky was getting up too, and in a hunched, not yet fully straightened posture, he looked up at him from under his brows. He didn't understand Alexey Alexandrovitch's feeling, but he sensed that it was something higher, and unattainable for him with his view of life.
